name: Regulatory discretion

subjectOf.text: Regulatory triggers generate the highest level of uncertainty and can produce ad hoc regulatory decisions and adverse market responses, so they are not the best option for contingent convertible bonds in executive compensation.
subjectOf.abstract: Regulatory triggers may lead to market uncertainty and ad hoc decisions by regulators and result in adverse market responses. Because regulatory triggers generate the highest level of uncertainty,152 they may not be the best option
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in Executive Compensation (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2097160

subjectOf.text: Institution specific automatic triggers in contingent capital securities are flexible and can be tailored to the parties' needs precisely because they operate independently of regulatory discretion.
subjectOf.abstract: Because institution-specific automatic triggers are independent from regulatory discretion, they have the advantage of being flexible and can be tailored to the parties' respective needs.
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857
scope_conditions: triggers are privately negotiated and automatic

subjectOf.text: The quantitative measures used in systemic risk assessment are not codified in statute, so the FSOC can alter its thresholds and its analysis through rulemaking.
subjectOf.abstract: the quantitative systemic risk assessment measures are not specifically codified and the FSOC can change thresholds and analysis via the rule making process
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Systemic Risk of Private Funds after the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2470008
